content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey with dumplings is a traditional dish where tender poultry meat is simmered in broth together with soft boiled dumplings made from dough. The meal is popular in Eastern European and Russian cuisines and is often served as a hearty winter lunch.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dumplings can be made from various doughs: wheat flour, buckwheat or potato puree.
In some Russian regions the dish is called “pelmeni in broth” or “homestyle dumplings”.
Typical broth seasoning includes bay leaf, whole black peppercorns and sometimes dried mushrooms for depth of flavor.
Turkey is used less frequently, but its lean meat gives the broth a lighter note.
The dish is commonly garnished with green onions, sour cream or mustard.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat (especially turkey)
items.content: Lean poultry helps maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal supplies B3, B6 and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The broth contains potassium, phosphorus and iron, important for muscle function and blood health.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: Dumplings add complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, keeping you full longer.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Broth is often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should control added salt.

items.title: Dumpling quality
items.content: White‑flour dumplings can be high in simple carbs; those with diabetes may prefer whole‑grain versions.

items.title: Meat handling
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can lead to bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, placing pieces of meat and dumplings in a deep bowl and ladling the aromatic broth over them. Optional toppings include fresh dill, parsley, sour cream or mustard.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months; reheat by bringing the broth to a boil.

content.title: About
content.content: Greens with ham or pork is a ready‑to‑eat mix of fresh leafy greens (spinach, lettuce, arugula) combined with selected pieces of ham or boiled pork. The product pairs the crisp texture of the greens with the savory, slightly salty flavor of the meat, making it a convenient option for quick lunches and snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of leafy greens and meat is a staple in Mediterranean cuisine.
The ham used is typically smoked, giving the mix a distinctive aroma.
Pork in the blend is usually pre‑cooked and diced for even distribution.
The product is often sold in vacuum‑sealed packs that keep it fresh for up to 7 days in the fridge.
Leafy greens provide vitamins A, C and K, while the meat adds protein and iron.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Ham or pork supplies high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from greens
items.content: Leafy vegetables are rich in vitamin K for blood clotting, as well as vitamin C and folate.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C and antioxidants from the greens help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The blend of protein and modest fat provides lasting satiety without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Pork contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains a lot of salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to pork or processed meat products.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: The product loses freshness quickly after opening; keep it refrigerated and consume within 3‑4 days.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives may be used to extend shelf life, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The mix is ready to eat: add it to salads, use as a sandwich filling, wrap in a flatbread, or toss into a quick vegetable omelet. For extra flavor, briefly sauté the mixture in a pan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. After opening, reseal tightly or transfer to an airtight container. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Hog maws are the edible stomach and esophagus of a pig, traditionally used in Southern US, Chinese, and Russian cuisines. After cooking they acquire a gelatinous texture, a mildly sweet flavor, and are commonly added to soups, stews, and fried snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hog maws are often called "pig intestines," though they are actually the stomach and part of the esophagus.
In the United States they are frequently deep‑fried into crunchy sticks, while in China they appear in aromatic broth dishes with soy sauce and ginger.
They are prized for long‑slow cooking, becoming tender and jelly‑like after several hours of simmering.
In some Russian regions they are served cold, marinated in vinegar and spices as a snack.
The high collagen content makes them popular in diets aimed at joint health.

items.title: Rich in collagen
items.content: Collagen supports skin elasticity, hair strength, and joint health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Hog maws provide animal protein useful for muscle repair and maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat cuts, they contain relatively little fat, fitting low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: They supply calcium, phosphorus, and iron, important for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Hydrating broth
items.content: When simmered, they release gelatin that helps maintain body fluid balance.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork products, including hog maws.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow pathogens such as Salmonella to proliferate.

items.title: High sodium in pickled versions
items.content: Pickled hog maws often contain a lot of salt, which is unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: Digestive difficulty
items.content: The dense gelatinous texture can cause stomach discomfort for some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hog maws are typically simmered for 2–3 hours until tender, then used in soups, stews, or deep‑fried. They can also be marinated in vinegar with spices and added to salads after cooking. Before preparation, rinse thoroughly and trim excess fat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh hog maws refrigerated at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for off‑odors; a sour or putrid smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft multigrain pretzels (3048) are tender yet slightly crunchy snacks made from a blend of wheat, rye, oat and barley. They have a mild sweet flavor, a lightly salted crust and a soft interior. Pretzels are suitable as a quick bite or as an addition to salads, soups, or cheese platters.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft pretzels originated in Germany in the 19th century as a milder alternative to traditional hard pretzels.
The multigrain mix boosts fiber content and makes the product more nutritious.
The classic “knot” shape symbolizes connection and friendship in German culture.
Pretzels are often served with mustard or cheese dips.
In some countries they are used as a base for open‑face sandwiches.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: The grain blend provides a high amount of fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Grains supply thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The combination of grains helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Pretzels offer a modest amount of protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: They contain magnesium, iron and zinc, essential for nervous and immune function.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People allergic to wheat, rye or barley should avoid these pretzels.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While softer pretzels are less calorie‑dense than some snacks, they should still be eaten in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed straight from the pack, added to salads, used in sandwiches, or served with dips (mustard, cheese, yogurt). They also work well cut into bite‑size pieces for canapés.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store in the refrigerator to retain softness and prevent drying out. Discard if pretzels become hard, moldy, or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice, fried, with chicken is a popular Asian dish consisting of boiled rice stir‑fried with pieces of chicken, vegetables and soy sauce. The dish offers a fragrant flavor, combining tender chicken with the subtle sweetness of rice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish is often cooked in a wok, allowing quick high‑heat stir‑frying of the ingredients.
In China there are many regional variations, where shrimp, beef or tofu replace the chicken.
Traditional recipes add thin strips of scrambled egg for extra taste and texture.
It is commonly garnished with sliced green onions and toasted sesame seeds.
Because it is fast and nutritious, it is a staple in cafeterias and street‑food stalls.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Rice delivers carbohydrates that are quickly converted into energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamin B6 and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iron, phosphorus and potassium, important for blood formation and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with moderate amounts of vegetable oil, the dish remains relatively low in saturated fats.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and added salt can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; ensure it is cooked thoroughly.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, often accompanied by soy sauce, chili sauce or a splash of vinegar. You can add fresh vegetables such as carrots, peas or bell pepper, and sprinkle with toasted sesame seeds and chopped green onions.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, make sure the dish reaches an internal temperature of at least 75 °C to eliminate any possible bacteria.

rice-white-with-tomatoes-and-or-tomato-b.title: White rice with tomatoes and/or tomato-based sauce, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: This is boiled white rice prepared with tomatoes or a tomato‑based sauce without any added fat. Rice provides complex carbohydrates, while tomatoes add flavor, aroma, and valuable nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is one of the most widely consumed grains worldwide.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives them their bright red color.
Cooking rice without fat keeps its caloric density low, making it diet‑friendly.
Fat‑free tomato sauce is often made from tomato puree, water, and spices.
The rice‑tomato combination is common in Mediterranean and Asian traditional dishes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a quick source of glucose needed for brain and muscle function.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Tomatoes are a good source of potassium, important for fluid balance.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Even fat‑free tomato sauce may contain salt; people limiting sodium should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice hot, mixed with tomato sauce or fresh chopped tomatoes. Add herbs, spices, or a splash of lemon juice to enhance flavor. It works well as a side dish for meat, fish, or vegetable meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Keep the tomato sauce separate, also refrigerated, for up to 5 days. Reheat thoroughly to at least 75 °C before serving.

turnip-greens-frozen-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Turnip Greens, Frozen, Cooked, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Turnip greens are the leafy tops of the turnip plant, a nutrient‑dense green vegetable. The frozen, cooked, no‑added‑fat version retains most of the vitamins and minerals while offering a convenient, ready‑to‑use product.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip greens belong to the Brassicaceae family, which includes broccoli, cabbage, and mustard.
They are rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support liver detoxification.
In the United States, frozen turnip greens are a common side dish in school cafeterias and fast‑food kitchens.
The raw leaves have a mildly bitter flavor that mellows with cooking.
Turnip greens contain more vitamin K per serving than spinach.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in turnip greens converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immunity.

items.title: Good source of folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during periods of rapid growth.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Minerals: calcium and iron
items.content: Calcium supports bone structure, while iron is vital for oxygen transport.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Turnip greens contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function when consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to Brassicaceae greens.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen cooked turnip greens can be added to soups, stews, salads, omelets, or served as a side dish. They reheat quickly in a skillet with a splash of water or broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C in its original packaging. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.
